hook_text: Every plate you sell before number ten belongs to the braai-stand man. Here's why.
clip_script: You want to sell pap-and-steak plates at the Saturday soccer tournament. Before plate number one, Saturday has already cost you: R340 for the braai stand, R220 for the gazebo and cooler boxes. R560 gone — and you have sold nothing. That is your pile of stones, and it does not care how your day goes. Every plate carries its own costs with it — steak, pap, chakalaka, container, R64 a plate. Sell at R120 and each plate leaves R56 in your pocket. That R56 is the contribution — not profit, not yet. It is one stone lifted off the pile. So the only question that matters while you set up: how many plates until the pile is gone? R560 divided by R56 — ten. Plates one to ten, you are working for the braai-stand man. Plate eleven is the first plate you sell for yourself. A backpack factory is the same sum with more zeros: a pile of R560 000, R56 a bag, survival line at 10 000 bags against a plan of 20 000. And when the butcher raises prices or a big buyer demands a discount, the line MOVES — so you calculate before you commit. Break-even is not a report card. It is a headlight.
visual_style: A tournament-day food stand with an actual pile of stones shrinking plate by plate, a chalk counter ticking to ten, then zooming out to a factory running the same sum in bigger numerals; smoky braai palette with headlight beams.
pacing: Stone-by-stone countdown, a triumphant beat at plate eleven, then quick what-if line shifts.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and find your own plate number ten.
